# Vatthugāthā (Snp 5.1 (PTS Snp 190))

**ID:** Snp 5.1 (PTS Snp 190)
**Section:** Suttanipāta (snp)

**Title (Pali):** Vatthugāthā
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0505m.mul4.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Vatthugāthā* ("Introductory Verses", Snp 5.1; verses 976–1031) constitutes the verse prologue to the *Pārāyanavagga*, the fifth vagga of the *Suttanipāta* [Norman 1983; Wynne 2007]. Comprising 56 verses composed predominantly in the Śloka metre (with verse 995 in mixed Triṣṭubh/Jagatī), it establishes the narrative setting of the entire book [Norman 1997-2001; Kingsbury 2002; Holt et al. 2003]. The narrative tells of the southern brahman ascetic Bāvarī, who dispatches sixteen of his disciples to the Buddha to inspect his marks and ascertain whether he is truly fully awakened [Goldstone 1978; Norman 1983; Holt et al. 2003].

Scholars consider these narrative introductory stanzas to belong to a later stratum than the core interrogations (*pucchā*) of the *Pārāyanavagga* [Kingsbury 2002; Wynne 2007]. Notably, while the *Cullaniddesa* comments on the subsequent question-suttas of the vagga, it contains no line-by-line glosses on the *Vatthugāthā*, indicating that these verses were either absent when the commentary was compiled or not yet treated as canonical scripture [Norman 1983; Hazra 1994; Wynne 2007]. The commentary *Paramatthajotikā* (Pj II), however, provides a commentary upon them and attributes their recitation to the elder Ānanda [Norman 1983; Norman 1997-2001; Holt et al. 2003].

Parallels and related narratives survive in Northern Buddhist traditions: a Sanskrit fragment includes the theme of Bāvarī and Kapilavastu along with the phrase *mūrdhnani pātam* and a list of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, though without an exact word-for-word alignment [Norman 1997-2001]. Text-reuse matches identified by DharmaNexus show that the verses are directly shared with the text printed in the *Cullaniddesa* (Cnd 1) and are quoted across commentarial works, including the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*, *Theragāthā-aṭṭhakathā*, and the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā* (Sīlakkhandhavagga), while automatic cross-language alignments connect thematic motifs with the Sanskrit *Lalitavistara* and Tibetan Mahāyāna treatises [DharmaNexus].
